module_title: Safe Handling and Hygiene for Shots and Teas

lessons.title: Washing roots thoroughly to remove soil and bacteria
lessons.body: Ginger and turmeric roots come out of the ground covered in soil, which can carry harmful bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli. To wash properly, start by filling a large basin with clean water. Add 1 tablespoon of salt and 2 tablespoons of white vinegar per 5 litres of water. This solution helps kill bacteria. Put the roots in and scrub each one with a clean vegetable brush or a new scouring pad. Pay attention to the knobs and crevices where soil hides. Scrub for at least 30 seconds per root. Then rinse under running clean water. If the water is very dirty, repeat the process with fresh water. For a final sanitising step, soak the roots in a solution of 1 teaspoon of household bleach (unscented, 3.5% concentration) per 4 litres of water for 2 minutes, then rinse again with clean water. This is especially important if you will not peel the roots. After washing, dry the roots with a clean cloth or let them air dry. Never wash roots in a river, stream, or stagnant poolâthese waters contain dangerous germs. Use only treated or boiled water. If you have many roots, wash them in small batches so the water stays clean. Change the water when it becomes muddy. Remember: clean roots mean safe shots and teas. Dirty roots can make your customers sick and ruin your business.

lessons.title: Personal hygiene practices before handling ingredients
lessons.body: Your hands, clothes, and body can carry germs that get into your ginger and turmeric products. Before you touch any ingredients, follow these steps: First, remove jewellery like rings, watches, and bracelets. Germs hide under them. Second, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds. Scrub between fingers, under nails, and up to your wrists. Use a nail brush to clean under your nails. Rinse and dry with a clean towel or air dryer. If you have a cut or wound on your hand, cover it with a waterproof plaster and wear clean gloves. Third, wear clean clothesâpreferably an apron that you only use for food preparation. Tie back long hair or wear a hairnet. If you are sick with diarrhoea, vomiting, or fever, do not handle ingredients. You can spread germs even if you feel only slightly ill. Also, avoid touching your face, phone, or money while working. If you must do so, wash your hands again. Keep your work area clean: wipe surfaces with a disinfectant before and after use. Use clean utensils and containers. Never sneeze or cough over the ingredients. If you need to taste, use a clean spoon and do not double-dip. These habits protect your customers and your reputation. In many African markets, customers watch how you handle foodâgood hygiene builds trust and repeat sales.

lessons.title: Avoiding cross-contamination with raw meats and utensils
lessons.body: Cross-contamination happens when harmful germs from raw meat, poultry, or fish transfer to your ginger and turmeric products. To prevent this, keep raw animal foods completely separate from your roots and brewing equipment. Use different cutting boards: one for raw meats (preferably red or marked) and another for roots and vegetables (green or white). Never use the same knife or board for both without washing and sanitising in between. After cutting raw meat, wash the knife, board, and counter with hot soapy water, then sanitise with a bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres water). Store raw meats in covered containers on the bottom shelf of your fridge or cooler, so juices cannot drip onto other foods. If you do not have a fridge, keep meats in a sealed bag away from roots. In your workspace, designate separate areas for preparing animal foods and plant foods. If space is tight, prepare roots first, then clean everything thoroughly before handling meats. Also, never use the same cloth to wipe surfaces that touched raw meat and then wipe your brewing area. Use disposable paper towels or separate cloths that you wash after each use. Utensils like spoons, funnels, and strainers used for your shots must be washed with hot soapy water and rinsed well. If you also sell meat or fish, do your ginger work first thing in the morning before any meat arrives. This reduces the risk. Remember: cross-contamination is invisible but dangerous. A single drop of raw meat juice can make your entire batch unsafe.

lessons.title: Using clean water sources for washing and brewing
lessons.body: Water is a major source of germs in drinks. You must use clean, safe water for washing roots, making shots, and brewing teas. The best water comes from a treated piped supply or a protected borehole. If you use well or river water, you must treat it first. Boiling is the most reliable method: bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes at high altitude). Let it cool before use. Alternatively, use a chlorine solution: add 2 drops of unscented household bleach (3.5% concentration) per 1 litre of clear water, stir, and wait 30 minutes. For cloudy water, first filter through a clean cloth, then use 4 drops per litre. You can also use commercial water purification tablets, following the instructions. Never use water that looks, smells, or tastes strange. For washing roots, use the same safe water. If you are connected to a municipal supply that is chlorinated, it is usually safe, but if there are boil-water advisories, always boil. For brewing teas, always start with safe water. Even if you boil the tea, starting with contaminated water can leave toxins that heat does not destroy. Store your clean water in clean, covered containers. Use a ladle or tap to take water outânever dip dirty cups into the storage container. Clean your water containers weekly with soap and rinse well. In many African communities, waterborne diseases like cholera and typhoid are common. Using clean water is not optionalâit is essential for your business and your family's health.

lessons.title: Safe disposal of peels and waste in your community
lessons.body: After peeling ginger and turmeric, you will have a lot of waste: peels, fibres, and used water. If not disposed of properly, this waste can attract flies, rodents, and cause bad smells. It can also spread germs if it contaminates water sources. Here is how to handle it safely. First, separate waste into categories: organic peels, plastic packaging, and dirty water. For organic peels, you can compost them. Dig a pit in your backyard at least 1 metre deep and 2 metres away from any well or water source. Add peels, cover with soil, and turn occasionally. After 2-3 months, you get rich compost for your garden. If you cannot compost, put peels in a sealed bag and take them to a designated dump site. Never dump peels in rivers, streams, or open drainsâthey block water flow and breed mosquitoes. For dirty water from washing, do not pour it directly onto the ground near your home. Instead, pour it into a soak pit or a drain that leads to a sewer. If you have no sewer, dig a small soakaway pit filled with gravel. For plastic waste, collect it and sell to recyclers or take it to a recycling centre. Never burn plasticâit releases toxic fumes. Keep your waste bins covered and empty them daily. Wash bins with soap and water weekly. In many African markets, community cleanliness is a shared responsibility. Organise with neighbours to have a regular waste collection or a communal compost site. Proper waste disposal keeps your community healthy and your business respected.

lessons.title: Recognising signs of spoiled batches and when to discard
lessons.body: Even with good hygiene, batches can spoil. You must know the signs so you do not sell unsafe products. For fresh ginger and turmeric shots, spoilage signs include: a sour or off smell, a fizzy or bubbly appearance (indicating fermentation), a change in colour (e.g., from bright orange to brown or dull), and a slimy texture. If you see mouldâwhite, green, or black fuzzy spotsâdiscard the entire batch. Do not try to scoop out the mould; the roots may already be contaminated. For teas, spoilage signs include: a cloudy appearance (if it was clear before), an unusual odour, or a film on the surface. If the tea has been sitting at room temperature for more than 2 hours, it is unsafe to drink. For both shots and teas, if you are unsure, throw it away. The rule is: when in doubt, throw it out. Never taste a spoiled batch to checkâyou could get sick. To prevent spoilage, store shots in clean, airtight bottles in the fridge for up to 3-5 days. If you have no fridge, keep them in a cool, dark place and sell within 24 hours. Add a squeeze of lemon juice to shots to slow spoilage. For teas, refrigerate and consume within 24 hours. Label each batch with the date and time of production. Use the oldest stock first. If a batch starts to spoil, discard it immediately and clean all containers and surfaces that touched it with hot soapy water and bleach solution. This protects your customers and your reputation. A single case of food poisoning can destroy your business.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Safe Handling and Hygiene for Ginger & Turmeric Shots and Teas

In the fast-growing African wellness beverage market, ginger and turmeric shots are a high-margin product with low barriers to entry. But the same moisture and nutrient profile that makes these roots valuable also makes them a perfect medium for bacterial growth. For a small processor in Nairobi, Lagos, or Accra selling to supermarkets, gyms, or export buyers, one spoiled batch can destroy a customer relationship, trigger a recall, and close access to formal retail. This reference module gives you the practical standards used by food-safe producers to protect both public health and your brand equity.

Contaminated product is not just a health risk â it is a business risk. Retailers in East and West Africa increasingly demand evidence of hygiene controls before listing a product. Buyers may ask for a food safety plan, water test results, or proof of staff training. The practices below are designed to be low-cost, locally adaptable, and auditable, so you can move from informal production to formal supply chains without expensive equipment.

1. Washing Roots Thoroughly to Remove Soil and Bacteria

Fresh ginger and turmeric arrive from farms carrying soil, organic matter, and a natural load of microorganisms. Soil is not just dirt â it can carry Salmonella, E. coli, and spore-forming bacteria that survive later processing. The objective of washing is to reduce this load before peeling and blending.

Use a three-stage wash system: a pre-rinse to remove bulk soil, a wash in potable water with a food-safe sanitiser if available, and a final potable water rinse. Never wash roots in a basin of standing water that becomes progressively dirtier â this recontaminates clean roots. Change water frequently, and scrub with a clean, dedicated brush that is not used for any other purpose.

2. Personal Hygiene Practices Before Handling Ingredients

Hands are the single most common route for pathogens to enter a beverage operation. A producer handling raw chicken at home and then peeling ginger without proper handwashing can transfer Campylobacter or Salmonella directly into your product. Personal hygiene must be treated as a non-negotiable production step, not a personal habit.

Establish a handwashing station at the entrance to the processing area with potable water, soap, and single-use towels or a clean cloth reserved for hands only. Wash hands for at least 20 seconds, including under nails, after using the toilet, after handling waste, after touching the face or phone, and after any break. Cuts and sores must be covered with waterproof dressings and, where possible, gloves. Jewellery, watches, and rings should be removed because they harbour soil and bacteria.

Clothing matters too. Wear clean aprons or overalls that are washed frequently, and tie back hair. If you are ill with vomiting or diarrhoea, do not handle product â this is one of the most common causes of contamination in small food businesses.

3. Avoiding Cross-Contamination with Raw Meats and Utensils

Cross-contamination occurs when bacteria from raw meat, poultry, or unwashed produce transfer to ready-to-eat products through shared surfaces, tools, or hands. In many African home-based processing setups, the same kitchen is used for family meals and commercial production. This is a major risk.

Separate your production space and time. If you cannot have a dedicated room, process ginger and turmeric before any raw meat is brought into the kitchen, then clean and sanitise all surfaces afterwards. Use colour-coded chopping boards and knives: one set for raw roots and produce, another exclusively for ready-to-eat items. Never use the same cloth for wiping meat surfaces and drying clean utensils.

Utensils must be washed in hot water with detergent, then sanitised. A simple bleach solution (following label instructions) or food-safe sanitiser can be used, followed by air drying. Store clean equipment off the floor and away from raw meat storage.

4. Using Clean Water Sources for Washing and Brewing

Water is both an ingredient and a cleaning agent in shot and tea production. If your water contains pathogens, your product will too. Boreholes, wells, and harvested rainwater must be tested at least annually for total coliforms and E. coli. In many African cities, municipal water is treated but can become contaminated in storage tanks or through intermittent supply.

If you rely on a borehole or well, treat water by boiling, filtration, or chlorination, and verify effectiveness with a test kit. For brewing, use water that meets drinking water standards. Store water in clean, covered containers and never use containers that previously held chemicals or fuel.

Table 1: Water quality parameters and recommended limits for beverage production
Parameter Recommended limit Why it matters
Total coliforms 0 CFU/100 ml Indicates contamination and possible pathogens
E. coli 0 CFU/100 ml Direct faecal contamination indicator
Turbidity < 5 NTU Cloudy water shields bacteria from disinfection
pH 6.5 â 8.5 Affects sanitiser effectiveness and product taste
Free chlorine (if chlorinated) 0.2 â 0.5 mg/l residual Ensures ongoing disinfection in storage

Source: WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, 4th edition (2022); Kenya Bureau of Standards KS EAS 12:2018 (Potable water).

5. Safe Disposal of Peels and Waste in Your Community

Ginger and turmeric peels are organic waste, but they can attract pests, create odours, and become a source of contamination if left near processing areas. In dense urban communities, improper disposal can also create friction with neighbours and local authorities, risking your operating licence.

Separate waste at the point of generation. Keep a covered bin with a lid in the processing area, lined with a bag that is changed daily. Never let waste accumulate near clean ingredients or packaging. Where possible, compost peels for urban gardens or supply them to local farmers as animal feed â this turns a disposal cost into a community benefit and strengthens your local reputation.

Do not pour wastewater from washing directly onto open ground or into storm drains. Use a designated drain or soak pit, and ensure it does not contaminate your own water source.

6. Recognising Signs of Spoiled Batches and When to Discard

Fresh ginger and turmeric shots have a short shelf life unless preserved. Spoilage can occur even with good hygiene if storage temperatures are too high or if the product is held too long. Recognising spoilage early protects customers and avoids costly recalls.

Signs to watch for include off-odours (sour, yeasty, or alcoholic), colour changes (browning, dulling, or separation that does not remix), gas formation in sealed bottles, mould growth on the surface or under the cap, and a slimy or stringy texture. Any of these means the batch must be discarded immediately. Do not taste a suspect batch â pathogens may be present without noticeable spoilage.

Table 2: Spoilage indicators and required action for ginger & turmeric shots
Indicator Likely cause Action
Sour or yeasty smell Fermentation by yeast or bacteria Discard entire batch; clean and sanitise equipment
Gas bubbles / swollen cap Microbial gas production Discard; check cold chain and shelf life
Mould on surface or cap Airborne spores, poor sealing Discard; review filling and storage
Colour separation that won't remix Emulsion breakdown or spoilage Discard if accompanied by off-odour
Bitter or fizzy taste Fermentation or oxidation Discard; do not sell

Source: FAO Manual on Simple Methods for the Detection of Foodborne Pathogens (2004); Codex Alimentarius General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969, revised 2020).

â  SAFETY WARNING â DISCARD, DO NOT SELL

If a batch shows any sign of spoilage â off-odour, gas, mould, or unusual texture â discard it immediately. Do not attempt to re-blend, re-bottle, or sell it at a discount. Selling spoiled product can cause serious illness and will permanently damage your brand and legal standing. In many African jurisdictions, food safety offences carry fines, closure orders, and criminal liability. When in doubt, throw it out.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Wash roots in three stages: pre-rinse, sanitised wash, potable rinse â never reuse wash water.
  • Wash hands for 20 seconds before handling ingredients; cover cuts and remove jewellery.
  • Use separate colour-coded boards and knives for raw roots and ready-to-eat items.
  • Test borehole/well water annually; use only potable water for washing and brewing.
  • Keep waste in covered bins, change daily, and compost or donate peels where possible.
  • Check every batch for off-odour, gas, mould, or texture changes before dispatch.
  • Maintain cold chain below 5Â°C for fresh shots and label with production and expiry dates.
  • Keep a simple daily hygiene log â buyers and inspectors increasingly ask for it.

Further Reading

  • WHO â Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, 4th edition (2022)
  • FAO â Manual on Simple Methods for the Detection of Foodborne Pathogens
  • Codex Alimentarius â General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969)
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â Food Safety Standards
  • African Union â Food Safety and Nutrition Resources

Business takeaway: Hygiene is not a cost centre â it is a market access strategy. Producers who can demonstrate safe handling, clean water, and traceable batch records are the ones who win supermarket contracts, export orders, and repeat customers. Build these practices into your daily routine now, and your brand will be ready for the next level of growth.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of salt and vinegar for washing ginger and turmeric roots?
options: A) 1 tablespoon salt and 2 tablespoons vinegar per 5 litres of water
B) 1 cup salt and 2 cups vinegar per 5 litres of water
C) 1 teaspoon salt and 1 teaspoon vinegar per 1 litre of water
D) 2 tablespoons salt and 1 tablespoon vinegar per 10 litres of water
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies 1 tablespoon salt and 2 tablespoons white vinegar per 5 litres of water.

quiz.q: Why should you scrub roots for at least 30 seconds per root?
options: A) To make them look shiny
B) To remove soil and bacteria from crevices
C) To soften the skin for peeling
quiz.explanation: Scrubbing for 30 seconds helps dislodge soil and bacteria hiding in knobs and crevices.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have a cut on your hand while handling ingredients?
options: A) Ignore it and continue working
B) Cover it with a waterproof plaster and wear clean gloves
C) Wash it with dirty water
D) Suck on the cut to clean it
quiz.explanation: Covering the wound and wearing gloves prevents germs from entering the food.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands before handling ingredients?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states to wash hands with soap and warm water for at least 20 seconds.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are sick with diarrhoea or vomiting?
options: A) Wear a mask and continue working
B) Take medicine and work anyway
D) Wash hands extra and work
quiz.explanation: Sick people can spread germs even if they feel only slightly ill, so they must not handle ingredients.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a good practice to avoid cross-contamination?
options: A) Use the same cutting board for raw meat and roots
B) Store raw meats above roots in the fridge
C) Use separate cutting boards for raw meats and roots
D) Wipe surfaces with the same cloth
quiz.explanation: Using separate cutting boards prevents germs from raw meat transferring to roots.

quiz.q: How should you sanitise a knife after cutting raw meat?
options: A) Rinse with cold water only
B) Wipe with a dry cloth
C) Wash with hot soapy water, then sanitise with bleach solution
D) Leave it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Hot soapy water and bleach solution kill harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: Where should raw meats be stored in a fridge?
options: B) Bottom shelf in covered containers
quiz.explanation: Storing raw meats on the bottom shelf prevents juices from dripping onto other foods.

quiz.q: What is the best way to treat water from a river or well?
options: A) Let it sit in the sun
B) Boil for at least 1 minute
quiz.explanation: Boiling for at least 1 minute kills most germs; at high altitude, boil for 3 minutes.

quiz.q: How many drops of unscented bleach (3.5%) per litre of clear water for purification?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states 2 drops per litre for clear water, and 4 drops for cloudy water after filtering.

quiz.q: Why should you not dip a dirty cup into a clean water storage container?
options: B) It can contaminate the entire container
C) It makes the water taste bad
quiz.explanation: Dipping dirty cups introduces germs that can multiply in the stored water.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to dispose of organic peels?
options: B) Burn them in the open
C) Compost them in a pit
quiz.explanation: Composting in a pit turns waste into useful compost and prevents pests.

quiz.q: How far should a compost pit be from a water source?
quiz.explanation: The lesson recommends at least 2 metres to prevent contamination of water.

quiz.q: What should you do with plastic waste from packaging?
options: C) Collect and sell to recyclers
quiz.explanation: Recycling is safe; burning plastic releases toxic fumes.

quiz.q: How often should you empty waste bins?
quiz.explanation: Daily emptying prevents flies, rodents, and bad smells.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a spoiled ginger shot?
options: B) Sour smell and fizzy appearance
quiz.explanation: Sour smell and fizz indicate fermentation or spoilage.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mould on a batch of shots?
options: A) Scoop out the mould and sell the rest
C) Add lemon juice to kill mould
D) Heat it to kill mould
quiz.explanation: Mould can produce toxins that spread through the batch, so discard all.

quiz.q: How long can fresh shots be stored in a fridge?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states shots can be kept in the fridge for up to 3-5 days.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have no fridge for shots?
options: A) Keep them in a cool, dark place and sell within 24 hours
B) Leave them in the sun
D) Store them in a metal pot
quiz.explanation: Without refrigeration, shots should be sold within 24 hours and kept cool.

quiz.q: Why should you label batches with date and time?
options: B) To use oldest stock first
quiz.explanation: Labeling helps you rotate stock and discard old batches before they spoil.

quiz.q: What is the bleach solution ratio for sanitising surfaces after raw meat?
options: A) 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres water
B) 1 cup bleach per 1 litre water
C) 1 teaspoon bleach per 10 litres water
D) 2 tablespoons bleach per 1 litre water
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies 1 tablespoon bleach per 4 litres water for sanitising.

quiz.q: Why should you remove jewellery before handling ingredients?
options: A) It can scratch the roots
B) Germs can hide under it
quiz.explanation: Germs can hide under rings and watches, contaminating food.

quiz.q: What should you use to dry your hands after washing?
options: B) A clean towel or air dryer
quiz.explanation: A clean towel or air dryer prevents recontamination.

quiz.q: How should you store clean water?
options: B) In a clean, covered container
quiz.explanation: Covered containers prevent contamination from dust and pests.

quiz.q: What is a soak pit used for?
quiz.explanation: A soak pit allows dirty water to drain safely into the ground.

quiz.q: What should you do before handling ingredients if you have long hair?
options: B) Tie it back or wear a hairnet
quiz.explanation: Tying back hair prevents it from falling into food.

quiz.q: Which water source is safest for brewing teas?
options: B) Treated piped water or boiled water
quiz.explanation: Treated or boiled water is free from harmful germs.

quiz.q: How long should you boil water at high altitude?
quiz.explanation: At high altitude, water boils at a lower temperature, so boil for 3 minutes.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a tea batch is spoiled?
options: B) Cloudy appearance and unusual odour
quiz.explanation: Cloudiness and off-odours indicate spoilage.

quiz.q: What should you do with a spoiled batch?
options: A) Sell it at a discount
B) Discard it and clean all containers
D) Add sugar to mask taste
quiz.explanation: Discard spoiled batches and sanitise to prevent contamination.
